claim: Commission guidance paras 148-149: class I important products (except those qualifying as FOSS under Art. 32(5)) need third-party assessment unless harmonised standards/common specifications/EUCC 'substantial' are applied; to use internal control '(i) all the applicable requirements of a relevant harmonised standard need to be applied; and (ii) the standard's scope needs to cover at least all the cybersecurity risks associated to that product's core functionality'

Commission guidance para 57 and Example 17: a paid edition or enterprise version under a commercial agreement is placed on the market 'irrespective of whether functionally equivalent software is also available free of charge under a free and open-source licence'; Example 17 is a FOSS operating system with a paid version, which is placed on the market
Commission guidance paras 44-46: only software that cumulatively (i) is under a licence granting the full Art. 3(48) rights and (ii) has openly shared source code qualifies as FOSS for the CRA

Commission guidance Example 58: a smartphone that integrates an operating system does not thereby have the core functionality of an operating system; mere integration does not make a product important or critical

Commission guidance paras 174-177: variants sharing architecture, security-relevant design and intended purpose may rely on a single risk assessment, technical documentation, conformity assessment and EU declaration; differences in software stacks, update mechanisms or remote connectivity must be reflected

Commission guidance paras 247-252: under Art. 69(1) EU type-examination certificates issued under other legislation (e.g. RED Delegated Regulation 2022/30) remain valid for the CRA for the risks they cover until 11 June 2028, including where the manufacturer voluntarily chose the notified-body procedure; gaps must still be assessed

Draft EN 304 626 V1.0.1 scope 1.3: hypervisors and container runtime systems (Annex III Class II point 1) and boot managers (Class I point 8) are covered by their own CRA harmonised standards; products embedding an OS with a different core functionality may use the draft as one part of demonstrating compliance

Draft EN 304 626 V1.0.1: both SP-REST and SP-GEN baselines list '(KEVD or KEVA)'; KEVD is documentation of how to update securely before or during first use; KEVA is an update mechanism operating by default with an easy opt-out; where alternatives are separated by 'or' at least one must be implemented with documented rationale

Draft EN 304 626 V1.0.1: MI-SUVI accepts signature verification, hash plus compensating controls, authenticated channel, controlled offline update or a verifying package manager (for image-based OSes installation means activating the new image); MI-SUDP requires a monotonic counter or equivalent anti-rollback; MI-SUAR exempts automated recovery after failed update or boot from explicit authorisation; UC-REST vs UC-GEN distinguishes restricted appliance OSes from general-purpose platforms

Draft EN 304 626 V1.0.1 MI-RTDL: where a product has documented real-time deadlines it 'shall demonstrate that its security mechanisms do not cause the product to exceed documented worst-case execution times for real-time tasks'
